lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Crops, Animals and Land in Different Farming Systems

pages.body:
Mr Tetteh grows only pineapples on ten hectares of land. His neighbour, Madam Abena, grows maize, cassava and beans on the same small plot and also keeps goats and chickens. Both are farmers, yet their farms look completely different.

- What crops and animals are found on the farms in your community?
- Why do you think some farmers keep animals and grow crops together while others do only one?

In Basic 7 you learned the names and characteristics of farming systems. A farming system is the way a farmer combines crops, animals and land, and manages them, to produce food and income. In this lesson we describe the combination of crops, animals and land in each system found in Ghana and weigh the advantages and disadvantages of each.
We begin with what is grown or kept, and how the land is used, in each system.

pages.title: Crops, animals and land combinations
pages.body:
| **Farming system** | **Crops** | **Animals** | **How the land is used** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monocropping | One crop only, such as maize, rice or pineapple, planted season after season | None | The same piece of land carries the same crop every season |
| Monoculture | One tree crop on a large area, such as cocoa, oil palm, rubber or cashew | None, or a few kept apart from the crop | A large plantation is used for one crop for many years |
| Mixed cropping | Two or more crops together, such as maize with cassava, or yam with okro and pepper | None | Different crops share one piece of land in the same season |
| Crop rotation | Different crops in a fixed order, such as maize, then cowpea, then cassava, then groundnut | None, or animals graze the plot when it rests | The land is divided into plots and the crop on each plot changes every season |
| Mixed farming | Food crops such as maize, cassava and vegetables | Poultry, goats, sheep, pigs or cattle | One part of the land is used for crops and another for animals on the same farm |
| Shifting cultivation and land rotation | Food crops such as yam, cassava, maize and plantain | Usually none | A plot is farmed for a few years and then left to rest as fallow while another plot is farmed |
| Pastoral farming | None, or a little fodder | Cattle, sheep and goats | Large areas of natural grassland are used for grazing |
| Agroforestry | Food crops grown between rows of trees such as cassia, teak or fruit trees | Sometimes small ruminants or bees | Trees and crops share the same land at the same time |

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Advantages and disadvantages of each system

pages.body:
In the forest zone of Ghana cocoa, oil palm, plantain and cassava are common, and mixed cropping and monoculture plantations are widespread. In the savanna zone farmers grow millet, sorghum, maize, yam and groundnut and keep cattle, sheep and goats, so mixed farming and pastoral farming are common. Along the coast vegetables, coconut and fish farming are important.

Next we weigh the good and the bad sides of each system.

pages.title: Advantages and disadvantages of each system
pages.body:
| **Farming system** | **Advantages** | **Disadvantages** |
|---|---|---|
| Monocropping and monoculture | Easy to manage and to use machines. The farmer becomes an expert in one crop. Large harvests can be sold to factories and for export | Pests and diseases of that crop build up. The soil loses the same nutrients each year. If the crop fails or the price falls, the farmer loses everything |
| Mixed cropping | If one crop fails, another can still be harvested. The soil is well covered, so erosion and weeds are reduced. Beans and other legumes add nitrogen to the soil. The family gets a variety of foods | Hard to use machines. Crops compete for light, water and nutrients. Harvesting and the control of pests are more difficult |
| Crop rotation | Soil fertility is maintained, especially when legumes are included. Pests and diseases are controlled because their host crop is absent for some seasons. Different root depths use nutrients from different soil layers | Needs good planning and knowledge of the crops. The farmer cannot grow the most profitable crop on all the land every year |
| Mixed farming | Animal droppings fertilise the crops and crop remains feed the animals. The farmer has income all year from more than one source. Risk is spread | Needs more money, labour and skill. Animals can destroy crops if they are not controlled. Diseases of animals bring extra cost |
| Shifting cultivation and land rotation | The soil recovers its fertility naturally during the fallow. Little money is needed for fertiliser | Needs a lot of land. Clearing and burning destroy forest and wildlife. It cannot feed a large, growing population |
| Pastoral farming | Uses land that is too dry or too poor for crops. Gives meat, milk, hides and manure | Overgrazing causes erosion. Herds may destroy crops, which leads to conflict between herders and crop farmers. Animals may lack water and feed in the dry season |
| Agroforestry | Trees protect the soil, give shade, add leaf litter and supply firewood, fruit and timber. Crops and trees use the land together | Trees take years to become useful. They may shade the crops and compete with them for water |

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: How the Components of a Farming System Support One Another

pages.body:
On Madam Abena's farm the chickens eat the maize bran left after milling. Their droppings are spread on the vegetable beds. The goats eat the cassava peels and groundnut tops, and their manure goes onto the maize plot. Almost nothing on the farm is thrown away.

- What does each part of this farm give to another part?
- How would the farm change if Madam Abena sold all her animals?

The parts of a farm are not separate. Crops, animals, the soil and the farmer depend on one another. In this lesson we explain how the components contribute to each other and how this keeps a farming system productive year after year, which is what we mean by sustainability.

We start with what the crops give to the animals, the soil and the farmer.

pages.title: What crops contribute
pages.body:
- Crops give food to the farm family and produce for sale.
- Crop residues such as maize stalks, groundnut tops, rice straw and cassava peels are feed for animals.
- Legumes such as cowpea, groundnut and soya bean have root nodules with bacteria that fix nitrogen from the air, which enriches the soil for the next crop.
- Leaves and roots left on the land decay into humus, which improves the structure of the soil and helps it to hold water.
- Cover crops and closely planted crops protect the soil from heavy rain, sun and erosion.
- Trees in agroforestry give shade, firewood, fruit and fodder and act as windbreaks.

Next we look at what animals give to the crops and the farmer.

pages.title: What animals contribute
pages.body:
- Animal droppings and farmyard manure return nutrients to the soil and reduce the need to buy fertiliser.
- Animals give meat, milk and eggs for food and for sale.
- Bullocks and donkeys supply draught power for ploughing and for carrying loads.
- Animals eat crop residues and weeds that would otherwise be waste.
- Animals are a store of wealth. A farmer can sell an animal when crops fail or when money is needed for school fees.
- Animal waste can be used to make biogas for cooking, and the slurry that remains is a good fertiliser.
- Bees pollinate crops and give honey.

[[pic: Cycle diagram of a mixed farm showing arrows from crops to animals labelled crop residues and feed, from animals to soil labelled manure, from soil to crops labelled nutrients and water, and from both crops and animals to the farm family labelled food and income.]]

Finally we link these contributions to the sustainability of each system.

questions.e: Animal droppings and farmyard manure return nutrients to the soil and reduce the need to buy fertiliser.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: How the components keep each system sustainable

pages.title: How the components keep each system sustainable
pages.body:
| **Farming system** | **How crops and animals keep it sustainable** |
|---|---|
| Mixed farming | Manure from the animals feeds the crops and residues from the crops feed the animals, so nutrients are recycled within the farm and little is bought from outside |
| Mixed cropping | Legumes add nitrogen for the cereals, tall crops shade or support climbing crops, and the ground cover protects the soil |
| Crop rotation | A legume in the rotation restores nitrogen used by the cereal, and changing the crop breaks the life cycle of pests and diseases |
| Shifting cultivation and land rotation | The wild plants that grow during the fallow return humus and nutrients to the soil before it is farmed again |
| Pastoral farming | The droppings of the grazing animals fertilise the grassland, and moving the herd allows the grass to grow again |
| Agroforestry | Trees bring up nutrients from deep in the soil and return them in leaf litter, while their roots hold the soil in place |
| Monocropping and monoculture | There is little recycling within the system, so the farmer must add fertiliser, plant cover crops and control pests to keep the land productive |

A sustainable farming system produces enough food and income today without damaging the soil, water and living things that farmers will need in the future. Systems in which the components support one another are usually the most sustainable.

> **Did you know?** On some farms in Ghana a poultry house is built over a fish pond. The droppings fall into the pond and feed tiny organisms that the fish eat, and the pond water is later used to water vegetables.

questions.q: A farming system is sustainable when it
o: Keeps the land productive for the future
Produces only one crop for export
Uses a new forest plot every year
Uses as much fertiliser as possible

pages.body:
- A farming system is the way a farmer combines and manages crops, animals and land to produce food and income.
- Monocropping and monoculture use the land for one crop. Mixed cropping grows two or more crops together. Crop rotation changes the crop on each plot in a fixed order.
- Mixed farming combines crops and animals on the same farm. Pastoral farming uses grassland for grazing animals. Agroforestry combines trees with crops.
- Each system has advantages and disadvantages. Growing one crop is simple and gives large harvests but carries a high risk, while mixed systems spread risk but need more labour and skill.
- Crops contribute food, income, crop residues for feed, nitrogen from legumes, humus and soil cover.
- Animals contribute manure, food, income, draught power and a store of wealth.
- A farming system is sustainable when its components support one another so that the land stays productive for the future.
